meta.title: Functional genomics of Buchnera and the ecology of aphid hosts
affiliations: Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona 85721, USA

abstractHtml: In many animal groups, mutualistic bacterial symbionts play a central role in host ecology, by provisioning rare nutrients and thus enabling specialization on restricted diets. Among such symbionts, genomic studies are most advanced for Buchnera, the obligate symbiont of aphids, which feed on phloem sap. The contents of the highly reduced Buchnera genomes have verified its role in aphid nutrition. Comparisons of Buchnera gene sets indicate ongoing, irreversible gene losses that are expected to affect aphid nutritional needs. Furthermore, almost all regulatory genes have been eliminated, raising the question of whether and how gene expression responds to environmental change. Microarray studies on genome-wide expression indicate that Buchnera has evolved some constitutive changes in gene expression: homologues of heat stress genes have elevated transcript levels in Buchnera (relative to other bacteria) even in the absence of stress. Additionally, the microarray results indicate that responses to heat stress and to amino acid availability are both few and modest. Observed responses are consistent with control by the few ancestral regulators retained in the genome. Initial studies on the role of host genes in mediating the symbiosis reveal distinctive expression patterns in host cells harbouring Buchnera. In the near future, a complete genome of pea aphid will accelerate progress in understanding the functional integration of aphid and Buchnera genomes. Although information for other insect symbioses is relatively limited, studies on symbionts of carpenter ants and tsetse flies indicate many similarities to Buchnera.

blocks.html: Many invertebrates possess endosymbiotic bacteria that are vertically transmitted from mother to progeny and that live in specialized organs. In his overview of animal symbioses, Buchner (1965) referred to these as ‘primary’ symbionts and proposed that their main function was to provision nutrients that were limiting in the diet of their hosts. In insects, such nutritional limitations are expected for a number of groups that have evolved specialized feeding habits, such as use of plant sap or vertebrate blood as the sole food. A variety of experimental studies, involving removal of native symbionts and/or manipulation of diets have provided support for nutrient provisioning by symbionts, especially for insect symbioses (e.g. Douglas & Prosser 1992; Sasaki & Ishikawa 1995; Febvay et al. 1999).

The use of molecular phylogenetic data has given robust confirmation to Buchner's general view that associations between insects and their primary symbionts extend into the deep evolutionary past, dating to the origins of major groups such as aphids, psyllids, leafhoppers, carpenter ants, and others. Repeatedly, such studies have revealed congruence between phylogenies of insect host and primary symbiont, corroborating that symbionts were important players in the diversification of insect groups that are dominant elements in modern terrestrial ecosystems. Thus, symbiosis was a prerequisite for the colonization of many specialized ecological niches and for the evolution of groups such as the sap-feeding and blood-feeding insects.

In recent years, the emergence of genomics has expanded our understanding of symbiotic associations of insects and bacteria. Because bacterial genomes are compact and rich in information regarding metabolic capabilities, the sequencing of complete genomes is relatively cost-effective. By providing a complete catalogue of genes and pathways present in organisms, the sequences themselves give a direct means of assessing functional contributions of symbionts to hosts. Genome sequences provide the foundation for the analyses of the transcriptome or proteome and provide the potential for assessing how symbiont functions are regulated in the context of the host environment.

The focus of this review is the best-studied insect–symbiont system, that of Buchnera aphidicola and its aphid hosts. Three genome sequences and several studies of genome-wide gene expression have been published. We summarize these results and relate them to some earlier, pre-genomics observations on aphid feeding and ecology. Together, these results suggest a role of Buchnera in both the expansion of aphid ranges and in constraints on their geographical and host-plant distributions. Additionally, we compare results from Buchnera genomes to those from two other ancient bacteriocyte-associated insect symbionts for which genome sequences are available.

sections.title: Gene content and genome sizes of symbionts

blocks.html: The first studies of symbiont gene content related to function in insect hosts were those of Baumann and coworkers, who cloned and sequenced fragments of the Buchnera chromosome from the aphid host Schizaphis graminum (Baumann et al. 1995). They documented the presence of pathways for several essential amino acids, confirming and extending previous evidence for a role of Buchnera in provisioning hosts with these nutrients. Most aphids feed exclusively on phloem sap, which contains limited amounts of essential amino acids; that is, the amino acids used in proteins that animals cannot synthesize themselves. These pathways are very well studied in bacteria, particularly in the model system of Escherichia coli. The close relationship between Buchnera and E. coli, and the clearly defined homology of their genes, was a major advantage in interpreting the new sequence data from Buchnera.

By the time the first Buchnera genome was published for the pea aphid Acyrthosiphon pisum (Shigenobu et al. 2000), it was known that Buchnera possessed genes for biosynthesis of most essential amino acids and that several of these genes (for synthesis of tryptophan, isoleucine, valine, leucine, and histidine) were transcribed (Baumann et al. 1995, 1999). Complete genome sequences are the only means of confidently showing what genes are absent from a genome, and the first Buchnera genome sequence was perhaps most notable for revealing which genes had been eliminated. These included most of those required for the synthesis of the nonessential amino acids, i.e. the amino acids that animal, such as the aphid hosts, can make themselves. This selective retention of particular biosynthetic genes demonstrated a striking complementarity between host and symbiont metabolic capabilities.

Bacterial genomes are tightly packed with genes, indicating that superfluous DNA is rapidly eliminated during evolution of bacterial lineages (Mira et al. 2001; Lerat et al. 2005). In symbiont genomes (and those of small genome pathogens), the loss of DNA is extreme, implying strongly that genes that are retained with intact reading frames are functionally significant to the organism. Other indicators are consistent with this inference: for example, different genes of a particular biosynthetic pathway are typically all lost or all retained, even when the genes are positioned in different parts of the chromosome.

Remarkably, the Buchnera gene set is a subset of that of E. coli and closely related bacteria. This fact suggests that, at least in the case of Buchnera, becoming symbiotic did not depend on acquiring novel genes. However, the Buchnera genome is highly derived and highly reduced, making it impossible to determine whether some genes enabling host invasion were involved in early stages of the symbiosis. Subsequent co-adaptation with the host genome may have rendered symbiont invasion genes obsolete. Some symbionts showing younger associations with insects, exemplified by Sodalis of tsetse flies, primary symbionts of Sitophilus weevils, and secondary symbionts of aphids, possess Type III Secretion Systems (Dale et al. 2001, 2002, 2005; Moran et al. in press), similar to those used by pathogenic bacteria to invade host cells. The underlying genes are known to be horizontally transferred in many cases, and their acquisition could be a step in the original evolution of an intracellular lifestyle. In Buchnera and other specialized symbionts, early utilization of such a system might be obscured by subsequent evolution of host mechanisms for ensuring infection of bacteriocytes (the cells housing the symbionts) and by ongoing reduction of the symbiont genome.

The extent to which genome contents of insect symbionts can be extended to infer metabolic capabilities is illustrated by the detailed analysis of Zientz et al. (2004), which elucidates the metabolic implications of the genomes of Buchnera, Blochmannia and Wigglesworthia.

Many symbionts, including Buchnera, have very large cell size: for example, the roughly spherical Buchnera cells are 3 µ in diameter and thus about 15× the volume of an E. coli cell. In Buchnera at least, this increase in volume is accompanied by amplification of the genome. In Acyrthosiphon pisum, individual Buchnera cells contain from 50 to over 100 chromosome copies, with the degree of amplification varying with life cycle stage (Komaki & Ishikawa 1999, 2000). The functional significance of the polyploidy is not clear: it may allow higher productivity per cell and it is presumably linked to the regulation of symbiont numbers within bacteriocytes, since it indicates a change in the coordination between chromosome replication and cell division.

sections.title: Plasmid location of nutrient biosynthetic genes

blocks.html: A remarkable early discovery was the finding that trpEG, the genes encoding the enzyme for the rate-limiting step of tryptophan biosynthesis, were encoded as tandem repeats on a plasmid and present in multiple copies relative to chromosomal genes in the Buchnera of many aphid species (Lai et al. 1994). Soon after, the genes for leucine biosynthesis were shown to occur on a different type of plasmid (Bracho et al. 1995). The two plasmids show different replication mechanisms and originated independently. The plasmid bearing the trpEG genes consist of a tandemly repeated unit of about 3.6 kb, with each unit containing an origin of replication containing binding sites for DnaA protein, similar to that on the chromosome of Buchnera and other related bacteria; the plasmid bearing the leu genes has its own replication proteins and is related to incompatibility plasmids in Salmonella and other bacteria. The amino acid biosynthetic genes occur on plasmids only in some Buchnera lineages. Plasmid-borne copies were acquired from the ancestral Buchnera chromosome and not from external sources (as for some plasmid-borne genes in bacteria) (Rouhbakhsh et al. 1996).

Overproduction and export of newly synthesized amino acids is a process distinctive of symbionts. Thus, Buchnera is highly unusual among bacteria in needing to overproduce tryptophan and leucine and is also unique in the amplification of the underlying genes and their location on plasmids. Presumably the two features are related: the unusual genomic arrangements most likely evolved as a means of increasing or regulating the expression of genes underlying these biosynthetic processes, to enable better provisioning of the end products to the hosts (Lai et al. 1994).

The initial interpretations of the plasmid position of these biosynthetic genes has been complicated by several additional findings. First, as mentioned, the Buchnera chromosome itself is present as many copies per cell, so plasmid-borne genes could be present in either more or fewer copies relative to single copy chromosomal genes. Both situations have been observed (Thao et al. 1998; Plague et al. 2003). Second, some of the genes on the plasmid are inactivated, sometimes highly truncated and sometimes only carrying small frame shifts and differing only slightly from intact copies (Lai et al. 1996; Wernegreen & Moran 2000). The latter are discernable only through cloning and individual sequencing of many copies from individual insects. In fact, trpEG pseudogenes, coexisting with intact copies, have been found in every species in which cloning and sequencing efforts were detailed enough to detect them. Thus, the extent of amplification of functionally relevant (intact and transcribed) copies is not easily determined. This obscures the meaning of studies of trpEG copy number in which numbers are determined by hybridization to a probe or by quantitative PCR, without extensive cloning (e.g. Birkle et al. 2002, 2004).

The number of copies of the plasmid-borne genes relative to chromosomal ones tends to be constant within a species but can differ considerably between species, ranging from less than 1 (e.g. Plague et al. 2003) to 24 (Thao et al. 1998). Some intraspecific variation has been identified as well. Furthermore, the movement of trpEG and leuABCD to a plasmid location occurred only once or very few times in evolution (Sabater-Muñoz et al. 2004), implying that the selection for plasmid location occurred in a common ancestor of a very large radiation of aphids that includes most modern species and a wide variety of feeding habits. Persistence of the plasmid arrangement does not indicate that it remains universally advantageous, but only that most rearrangements are not tolerated in Buchnera genomes. This is suggested by the fact that Buchnera chromosomes are extremely static, showing a lower incidence of rearrangements relative to sequence divergence, than any other bacterial group (Tamas et al. 2002; van Ham et al. 2003). Thus, once the genes were transferred to the plasmid, they may persist there even if the original benefit of the plasmid location is removed.

Although gene order and orientation have been stable for more than 100 million years (Myr) of Buchnera evolution, comparison of the three available genome sequences reveals ongoing deletions and inactivation of ancestral genes in each lineage (Tamas et al. 2002; van Ham et al. 2003). Furthermore, some of the observed gene losses are expected to impact host ecology. For example, Buchnera of Schizaphis graminum possesses degenerate copies of the genes underlying incorporation of inorganic sulphur; the coding regions for several of the required enzymes are disrupted by stop codons and deletions, suggesting recent inactivation (Tamas et al. 2002). Because grasses, the host plants of S. graminum, contain high amounts of sulphur-containing organic compounds, they are likely to ingest homocysteine or related sulphur-containing intermediates, enabling the production of methionine and cysteine without incorporation of inorganic sulphur. Similar losses have occurred in two of the sequenced genomes; e.g. Buchnera of Baizongia lacks the pathway for arginine and pantothenate biosynthesis, whereas it retains genes underlying biotin biosynthesis that are eliminated from genomes of the Buchnera of both S. graminum and Acyrthosiphon pisum (van Ham et al. 2003).

Such inactivations are the likely explanation for strain-specific dietary requirements in aphids. A review of aphid nutritional physiology (Srivastava 1987) summarizes earlier studies of dietary requirements for amino acids and concludes that aphids ‘appear to constitute a rare group where different insect populations within one species differ in their requirement for essential amino acids.’ For example, certain A. pisum biotypes (representing individual clonal isolates with distinctive host plant use) have dietary requirements for particular essential amino acids, including arginine, phenylalanine, tryptophan and valine, based on studies of aphids with intact symbionts (Srivastava et al. 1985; Srivastava 1987). The ability of sulphate to spare the requirement for sulphur-containing amino acids was another variable in dietary requirements of A. pisum genotypes (Srivastava 1987). Additionally, Aphis fabae clones grown on defined diets differ in their amino acid requirements, with individual clones (with symbionts intact) requiring histidine, methionine, threonine, or valine for optimal growth (Wilkinson & Douglas 2003). These observations strongly suggest that Buchnera inhabiting particular aphid lineages differ in biosynthetic capabilities due to mutational inactivation of particular pathways.

Because Buchnera genomes show no cases of gene uptake, such loss of function is almost certainly irreversible, at least once a pathway is inactivated by more than one mutation. An implication is that Buchnera acts as a potential constraint on the long-term ecological diversification of aphid hosts. For example, loss of the pathway for sulphur fixation implies that S. graminum is now destined to remain on grasses, or other hosts with sufficient sources of fixed sulphur, for its entire evolutionary future (Tamas et al. 2002). The extent of such inactivations as a basis for polymorphism within a species is not clear from the genomic sequences. For S. graminum and A. pisum, the Buchnera genomes were sequenced for a single aphid genotype. For Buchnera of Baizongia pistaciae, a population sample was used, and the resulting genomic sequence revealed five polymorphic sites that may represent snapshots of recent gene inactivations.

Thus, several lines of evidence indicate that Buchnera genome evolution results in the ongoing loss of capabilities for provisioning hosts and never in the acquisition of new capabilities. It may appear puzzling that symbionts lose capabilities that might benefit their mutualistic hosts. Because plants, and plant parts, vary in phloem content of amino acids (Sandström & Moran 1999; Koyama et al. 2004), aphid colonies living on a particular plant may experience local relaxation of selection for retention of the corresponding Buchnera pathway. Furthermore, the mutational target resulting in inactivation of the pathway can be quite large, especially for the longer pathways requiring more enzymes, increasing the likelihood of loss during a particular period of relaxed selection. The fact that Buchnera of major aphid lineages retain capacity for biosynthesis of most or all of the essential amino acids implies that losses of particular pathways are deleterious in the longer run and generally lead to lineage extinction.

sections.title: Transfer of bacterial genes to host genome?

blocks.html: Full genome sequences of animals and plants have produced recent revelations regarding the large extent of gene transfer from ancestral organelles to the nuclear genome (Martin 2003). Buchnera resembles organelles in many ways, including ancient derivation from a free-living bacterium, obligate residence within the host cytoplasm, and large-scale genome reduction, raising the possibility that Buchnera has also transferred genes to the host genome. But, in contrast to mitochondria and chloroplasts, it is not apparent that Buchnera must import gene products from its host for the processes underlying its own replication; the gene inventories from the completed genomes indicate that it retains its own polymerases and other basic cellular machinery. In fact, aside from the retention of nutrition-provisioning genes, the genome reduction in Buchnera is similar to that observed in obligate pathogens with small genomes, such as mycoplasmas and rickettsiae, organisms that are horizontally transferred among hosts and that are generally deleterious. All of these organisms are parasites in the sense of requiring host metabolic products, but the genome reduction of the pathogens implies that extensive gene loss can occur without dependence on products of genes transferred from symbionts to the host genome. (Selection on hosts would not maintain genes for the benefit of pathogens.)

One reason that Buchnera and similar mutualistic symbionts of animals might differ from organelles in the extent of gene transfer to the host germ line is that the obstacles to such transfer are more formidable. Whereas mitochondria and chloroplasts originated in single-celled ancestors, enabling close proximity between their genomes and host nuclear genomes, Buchnera is confined to non-germ-line cells except for brief stages in the life cycle following egg infection. Despite these caveats, gene transfer cannot be excluded as a possibility. Indeed, transfer to the host nucleus of a chromosomal segment of a Wolbachia symbiont appears to have occurred in a beetle (Kondo et al. 2002), indicating that such events are possible. The sequencing of the Acyrthosiphon pisum genome, expected within the near future, will largely answer this question, at least for the case of Buchnera.

Reduced bacterial genomes typically possess very few regulatory genes, and this generalization extends to Buchnera, which retains only about five of the more than 200 regulatory genes found in E. coli. Additionally, the organization of transcription units is highly disrupted by the loss of genes and by rearrangements (Moran & Mira 2001). Finally, the distinctive biology of symbionts, which live in a relatively constant environment and which overproduce some metabolic products for hosts, is expected to impose distinctive selection pressures on gene regulation. In most bacteria, such as the well-characterized E. coli, genes are transcribed in discrete transcription units (operons) with a high level of independence of expression, choreographed by a large set of regulatory elements, including both proteins and RNAs. In contrast, Buchnera does not show clearly defined transcriptional terminators, and the binding sites for the generalized sigma-70 promoter, required for initiation of transcription for most genes, are not readily distinguished.

Although the inability to culture Buchnera makes genetic manipulations impossible, analysis of gene expression patterns is possible, using RNA extracted from aphids and symbionts. The full genome sequences for Buchnera have allowed the examination of global gene expression levels using gene microarrays. Such studies, summarized below, can reveal the extent to which Buchnera responds to ecologically realistic environmental change.

sections.title: Changes in constitutive expression — heat shock genes

blocks.html: An early puzzle in Buchnera biology was the extremely high levels of a protein that was initially named ‘symbionin’ and hypothesized to play a central role in the aphid–bacterial interaction (Ishikawa 1982). Later, once sequencing was available, symbionin was determined to be GroEL protein (orthologue of HSP60), a chaperonin that is universally distributed and that functions in the folding of new and destabilized proteins (Ohtaka et al. 1992). This protein comprises about 10% of Buchnera protein under non-stress conditions (Baumann et al. 1996), a level equivalent to that in E. coli under the most elevated state, as induced by heat or other stresses that cause proteins to destabilize. Furthermore, full genome microarrays have revealed that most of the 20 homologues of heat shock genes retained in the Buchnera genome are overexpressed constitutively compared to their levels in other bacteria (Moran et al. 2003; Wilcox et al. 2003; Fig. 1). Together, these gene products are involved in recycling and refolding proteins that have become degraded. The overexpression of this set of genes, which are dispersed on the Buchnera chromosome, indicates a general compensation for problems with protein stability (Wilcox et al. 2003). Because Buchnera shows accumulation of mutations effecting amino acid changes throughout the genome, due to relaxed selection or ineffective selection resulting from small genetic population size, this constitutive overexpression is best explained as a compensatory adaptation to mutational destabilization of proteins (Moran 1996). Experiments in E. coli and other organisms demonstrate that overexpression of GroEL and other chaperonins can mask mutations that would otherwise be deleterious (e.g. Rutherford & Lindquist 1998; Fares et al. 2002).

sections.title: Reduction in regulatory mechanisms controlling transcription

blocks.html: As noted above, an observation applying to all highly reduced bacterial genomes and to the Buchnera genomes in particular, is the extensive loss of regulatory genes. Inspection of the genome sequence does not reveal any obvious new regulatory mechanisms, but these would likely not be recognizable and might be expected in view of the fact that Buchnera has co-evolved with hosts for over 100 Myr.

Full genome microarrays for Buchnera, consisting of individually amplified double-stranded DNA sequences, allow direct evaluation of global transcriptional responses to environmental challenges. To date, these studies have been carried out for two kinds of changes that routinely affect naturally occurring aphids and their Buchnera: heat stress and fluctuations in the composition of dietary amino acids. Both studies indicate that transcriptional responses are few and consist only of ancestral responses that have been retained.

Responses to heat shock indicate that, in addition to overexpression under non-stress conditions, Buchnera of Schizaphis graminum does retain a modest heat shock response involving a global heat shock regulator and four promoters affecting expression of six genes (Fig. 1, Wilcox et al. 2003). The regulatory mechanisms appear to be the same as in E. coli, and the consensus heat shock promoter is the same. As mentioned, most of the heat shock gene homologues have lost heat shock promoters and are overexpressed constitutively.

For considerations of host nutritional ecology, the expression of Buchnera's amino acid biosynthetic genes is of particular interest. Amino acid profiles in phloem differ among plant species and also among growth stages of individual plants (e.g. Sandström & Moran 1999; Koyama et al. 2004), implying fluctuations in the need for different biosynthetic contributions by Buchnera. In E. coli and related bacteria, these pathways have a total of 16 different specific transcriptional regulators. Buchnera of S. graminum retains only one of these, metR, which is a regulator of metE, underlying methionine synthesis; in Buchnera of Acyrthosiphonpisum, metR is inactivated through several frame shifts and a large deletion. Experiments manipulating amino acid levels in the plants and aphids showed that transcript levels of these genes lack responses that are statistically significant and substantial (greater than twofold), with the striking exception of metE (Fig. 2; Moran et al. 2005). The metE transcript was significantly up-regulated with the addition of several nonessential amino acids, which may be equivalent for Buchnera physiology due to interconversions in aphid tissues (Moran et al. 2005). Experiments using reverse transcriptase quantitative PCR confirmed that metE expression is most sensitive to levels of homocysteine, demonstrated to be a co-activator of metR in E. coli. Furthermore, the response was completely lacking in Buchnera of A. pisum, in which metR is degraded.

Thus, Buchnera has lost almost all mechanisms for regulating transcript levels of genes underlying amino acid biosynthesis in response to amino acid pools. Moreover, it has not invented new ones during the course of its evolution in aphid hosts, at least none with substantial effects on transcript levels. In Buchnera of S. graminum, the only strong response to amino acid fluctuations is dependent on the single retained regulator (metR), and even that system is missing from both of the other sequenced Buchnera genomes (van Ham et al. 2003).

The few regulatory genes that Buchnera retains may control shifts in gene expression corresponding to different stages of its life cycle within hosts. A period of rapid division and distinctive gene expression appears to follow colonization of a new host embryo (Wilkinson et al. 2003), and later growth of the Buchnera population closely tracks growth of the host (Baumann & Baumann 1994). These observations indicate that distinct phases do occur in the Buchnera life cycle, and these are expected to correspond to distinct phases of gene expression. Homologues of himA (encoding Integration Host Factor) are intact in all three Buchnera genomes; in other bacteria, this gene is involved in detecting changes in the cellular environment and switching gene expression accordingly. In Buchnera, himA may be involved in the switch between life cycle stages, such as replicative stages and vegetative stages, during which cells are metabolizing and producing nutrients for hosts but not dividing.

The overall picture of gene expression is that it is relatively static, compared to free-living bacteria. Additionally, transcription units are less clearly defined. For example, heat shock increases transcription of heat shock genes as well as downstream sequences, even when the downstream genes are on the complementary strand (Wilcox et al. 2003).

Analyses of Buchnera genomes and gene sequences are consistent with the occurrence of elevated levels of genetic drift (Moran 1996; van Ham et al. 2003; Rispe et al. 2004). In particular, sequence analyses consistently indicate rapid sequence evolution. However, polymorphism in Buchnera genes within host species is extremely low, as is polymorphism in aphid nuclear genes. Low intraspecific polymorphism reflects the typical population structure of aphids, which are clonal during most of their life cycle, highly mobile and subject to large-scale bottlenecks within a geographical region (Funk et al. 2001; Abbot & Moran 2002).

Shifts in selection on the pathways underlying amino acid production are suggested by the few studies comparing closely related species. For example, Diuraphis species that differ in the extent of damage inflicted on host grasses also differ in the presence of pseudogenes for tryptophan biosynthesis (Wernegreen & Moran 2000). Also, Buchnera of the genus Uroleucon appear to have undergone relaxation of selection on some amino acid biosynthetic pathways, with elevated sequence evolution and the appearance of pseudogenes in some lineages (Wernegreen et al. 2000). These comparisons of closely related species provide a picture of the initial stages of gene and pathway loss, leading to major differences in content of provisioning abilities between divergent lineages, as revealed by the complete genome sequences (Tamas et al. 2002; van Ham et al. 2003).

The functioning of an intimate symbiont such as Buchnera cannot be understood without addressing, at the molecular level, its integration within hosts. This aspect has been relatively neglected until recently, due to the lack of information on the aphid genome. However, one recent study has addressed coordination of aphid gene expression with that of Buchnera. Nakabachi et al. (2005) characterized transcripts that were differentially expressed in Acyrthosiphon pisum bacteriocytes. The findings reinforce the view of the bacteriocyte as a factory for amino acid metabolism, requiring the coordination of host and symbiont contributions. Aphid genes with high transcript levels in bacteriocytes relative to other tissues included those underlying processes of amino acid transamination, catabolism and transport. Other up-regulated genes included homologues of genes encoding transporters and lysozymes that act to degrade bacterial cell walls. These findings may be relevant to outstanding mysteries regarding Buchnera function: how small molecules are moved between host and symbiont, as required for the nutritional exchange which has been demonstrated in physiological studies, and how symbiont numbers are regulated. The Buchnera genome lacks most homologues of genes encoding transporters, including ones used by related bacteria to move amino acids across cell walls. Gene expression profiles obtained for bacteriocytes raises the possibility that host transporters interact with bacterial membranes so as to effect movement of amino acids or other metabolites.

Recent studies have begun to shed light on the gene expression underlying specification of the bacteriocytes during early development (Braendle et al. 2003). These data indicate that the Buchnera inoculum is a major feature of early embryogenesis. Bacteriocytes are determined and colonized at an early stage, and no further host cells are recruited to this role later.

These developmental specializations presumably reflect a long history of co-evolution. The most plausible view is that aphids acquired these symbionts only once, early in their evolution, enabling them to exploit a novel ecological niche, phloem-feeding on vascular plants. Such a lifestyle would be untenable without symbionts, due to nutritional inadequacies. Co-adaptation on the part of the aphids subsequently rendered them dependent on Buchnera for reasons other than the nutritional dependence that was the original basis for the association. In modern aphids, early development is disrupted if Buchnera is removed using antibiotics, and even nutritional supplementation does not remove the requirement for Buchnera during embryonic development (Buchner 1965; Douglas 1998). Thus, the hosts require the symbionts, even as they lose capabilities to provide nutrients and to regulate production of these nutrients in response to host needs. Mutations in the aphid genome can also affect essential processes, but these can be restored by sex and recombination, whereas the dependence on a mutation-prone, asexual genome may constitute a major limitation on aphid evolution. Possibly secondary symbionts sometimes replace nutritional functions of Buchnera; however, known contributions of secondary symbionts are not nutrient related (Montllor et al. 2002; Oliver et al. 2003).

The planned sequencing of the A. pisum genome will vastly accelerate understanding of how host and symbiont genomes function together. A particularly unknown arena is that of the host immune system which must be modulated to allow the proliferation of bacteria within the host body. Additionally, the regulation of symbiont numbers must be controlled in some manner by the host; as yet, the mechanisms are unknown.

Building on the success and insights provided by studies of the aphid–Buchnera association, genomic approaches have been applied to several other associations of insects with intracellular bacteria. To date, three more full genome sequences have been completed for two of these symbionts, Blochmannia species, from carpenter ants, and Wigglesworthia glossinidius, from tsetse flies (Akman et al. 2002; Gil et al. 2003; Degnan et al. 2005). Remarkably similar patterns of genome evolution have occurred in all three symbiont lineages (Buchnera, Blochmannia and Wigglesworthia); these include drastic reductions in genome size and gene content, extreme AT bias, and elevated rates of nucleotide substitutions. The repeated emergence of these features in these and other intracellular mutualists and pathogens suggests that prolonged intracellular associations enforce similar shifts in selective pressures and population structure.

The precise evolutionary steps underlying reductive genome evolution in these symbionts are still unclear; however, growing evidence suggests that an innate deletional bias of bacterial genomes combined with the proliferation of repeat elements (e.g. transposons) facilitate the process (Mira et al. 2001; Moran & Plague 2004). As a result of these processes, genomes of both Wigglesworthia and Blochmannia have shrunk to less than one-fifth the size of that of E. coli. As is typical in small genome bacteria, all three groups retain a core set of metabolic proteins; in fact, 331 genes, or slightly over half of the genes of each genome, are shared between Buchnera, Blochmannia, and Wigglesworthia. Each symbiont also contains genes not found in the other two.

Both sequenced Blochmannia genomes retain a suite of essential amino acid biosynthetic pathways similar to that of Buchnera, as well as the pathways involved in the production of several additional cofactors, and urea degradation (Fig. 3; for a review see Zientz et al. 2004). In contrast, Wigglesworthia has lost nearly all amino acid biosynthetic capabilities but retains the genes involved in producing a number of cofactors including B complex vitamins (e.g. thiamine, biotin, pyridoxine; Fig. 3). Neither Blochmannia strain retains any plasmids, and the single plasmid found in Wigglesworthia does not encode any genes known to be involved in either amino acid or cofactor biosynthesis (rep, speG, traT, ybbK, yggB, ibp; Akman et al. 2002). The nutritional contribution of the latter endosymbiont to the tsetse hosts is consistent with the composition of mammalian blood, which is rich in protein but poor in such vitamins (Nogge 1981). Many carpenter ants (Camponotus, Colobopsis, and Polyrhachis) are omnivorous; thus, Blochmannia’s contribution of essential amino acids and cofactors is somewhat unexpected. Their metabolic contribution might be significant for temporary phases of larval or pupal development or for seasonal periods during which ants are heavily dependent on plant exudates (Degnan et al. 2004; Wolschin et al. 2004).

The recent completion of the Blochmannia pennsylvanicus genome has permitted comparison within and between two phylogenetically and compositionally unique symbiont lineages (Bl. pennsylvanicus–Bl. floridanus and Buchnera of the three aphid species; Degnan et al. 2005). As in the three Buchnera genomes, Bl. pennsylvanicus and Bl. floridanus exhibit complete conservation of gene order, differences in gene content are strictly due to irreversible gene losses, and Blochmannia shows extremely high rates of protein evolution. These parallels reinforce conclusions from studies on Buchnera regarding the processes involved in genome erosion of obligate intracellular bacteria. In particular, the dramatic reduction in genome size appears to have occurred very early in both symbioses, in part as a result of relaxed selection on metabolic pathways that are redundant in the host cell.

Some differences in genome content probably reflect biological differences among these three symbiont groups. Phylogenetic analyses indicate different ages of their obligate host associations of Buchnera, Blochmannia, and Wigglesworthia (150–250 Myr, 30–40 Myr, and 50–100 Myr, respectively; Moran et al. 1993; Akman et al. 2002; Degnan et al. 2004). Also, Wigglesworthia and Blochmannia both exist freely in the host cell cytoplasm and retain a rodlike morphology (Aksoy 1995; Sauer et al. 2000), in contrast to Buchnera, which is large, spherical and surrounded by a host-derived membrane. Blochmannia and Wigglesworthia cells have been observed to be quite long (12–30 µm and 5–9 µm, respectively), although polyploidy has not yet been noted.

The wealth of genomic data for the symbionts has generated interest in transcriptional analyses of the host insects. Transcriptome and full genome analyses are underway for the tsetse fly, vector for African trypanosomes (> 60 000 ESTs for Glossinia moristans; Aksoy et al. 2005), and limited expression data are becoming available for carpenter ants (Goodisman et al. 2005).

Genomic studies of Buchnera reveal small genomes that have lost and continue to lose many capabilities, including those for provisioning hosts and for regulating gene expression. This genetic erosion must occur in the context of ongoing co-adaptation by hosts, the nature of which has yet to be characterized. One of the most intriguing of the many remaining issues regarding the functional genomics of symbiosis is the question of how host gene products interact with symbionts to compensate for gene losses and to integrate symbiont functions into the mutualistic system. For example, we do not know the answer to the question of whether different Buchnera lineages could be transferred among divergent species of aphids successfully or whether symbionts and hosts show specialized co-adaptation that would prevent such transfer. In the next few years, we can hope for major advances in this relatively unknown area, due to the planned completion of the genome of the model host species, Acyrthosiphon pisum.

Nancy Moran and Patrick Degnan both study the genomics of bacterial symbiosis in animals. The main study systems are aphids and other sap-feeding insects. These insects contain a variety of heritable bacteria, which affect host nutrition, resistance to natural enemies, and tolerance to thermal stress.
